ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act 2009); Companies Act 1993; Tax Administration Act 1994; Financial Markets Authority (FMA) and Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) AML/CFT Supervision Guidelines; New Zealand Gazette and Companies Office Name Registration Rules; Privacy Act 2020; New Zealand Sanctions Act 2022; Terrorism Suppression Act 2002; and the Companies (Foreign Company) Regulations 2017 where applicable.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: certified copy from the New Zealand Companies Office, then Apostille issued by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs (Authentications Unit). Consular legalization path (non-Apostille member state): authentication by the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs, followed by consular legalization at the relevant foreign embassy or consulate in New Zealand. The two paths are parallel and mutually exclusive; do not chain Apostille and consular legalization sequentially.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing (Certificate of Compliance)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path for member-state recipients: request Certificate of Compliance from Companies Office, obtain Apostille from the Department of Internal Affairs Authentications Unit. Consular legalization path for non-member states: Department of Internal Affairs authentication, then consular legalization processing through the destination country's diplomatic mission in New Zealand. Choose only one path according to the recipient country.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution / Power of Attorney for incorporation and banking signatories
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public in the jurisdiction of execution, endorsed by the proposed directors and/or shareholders of the New Zealand company
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: notarization of signatures by a local notary, follow by Apostille from the competent authority of the notary's jurisdiction (if an Apostille Convention member). Consular legalization path: notarization, authentication by the foreign ministry or equivalent authority of the notary's jurisdiction, then legalization by the New Zealand embassy/consulate in that jurisdiction. The two paths are mutually exclusive; never sequentially combine Apostille and consular legalization.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Articles of Association (Constitution of the Limited Company)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: The founding shareholders/directors of the proposed New Zealand company, typically certified by the New Zealand counsel or by a notary public
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: if executed in New Zealand, notarize the execution page and obtain an Apostille from the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs. If executed overseas in an Apostille member state, obtain a notarial certificate and the relevant domestic Apostille in that state. Consular legalization path: in non-member states, notarize, obtain competent national authentication, then complete consular legalization at the New Zealand embassy/consulate. Do not chain Apostille and consular legalization.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Bank Reference Letter (banker's reference from the sponsoring bank or principal financial institution)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: The financial institution where the founding shareholders, trust settlor, or ESOP sponsor maintain an active banking relationship
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: bank officer's signature is notarized, followed by Apostille from the designated competent authority of the bank's jurisdiction if it is an Apostille Convention member. Consular legalization path: notarization and competent public authentication, followed by consular legalization at the New Zealand embassy/consulate in that jurisdiction. Selection of path depends solely on the destination country's membership in the Apostille Convention; the paths are never combined.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Before incorporation and on an ongoing basis, the responsible New Zealand reporting entity must conduct enhanced due diligence screening of all directors, shareholders, beneficial owners, ESOP trustees, and employee-beneficiaries exceeding 25% ownership. Screening must cover the New Zealand Sanctions Act 2022 sanctions lists, United Nations Security Council Consolidated Lists, OFAC SDN and non-SDN sanctions lists, HM Treasury sanctions lists, FATF public statements and high-risk jurisdiction lists, and New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) watchlists. All individuals identified as Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), their immediate family members, and known close associates must trigger senior-management approval, source-of-wealth review, source-of-funds verification, and enhanced transaction monitoring. Screening must be repeated at least every 90 days and upon any material change in ownership, control, or trust structure. Negative news and adverse media searches must be performed on the entity and all underlying principals. Any sanctions hit, PEP determination, or red flag requires immediate escalation to the AML/CFT compliance officer, potential filing of a Suspicious Transaction Report to the New Zealand Police FIU, and prohibition of any transaction involving a sanctioned individual or entity.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office (www.companiesoffice.govt.nz) including the 'Company Name Availability Check' and online incorporation / name reservation portal
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: New Zealand company names must be expressed in Latin characters; names using te reo Maori are permitted with proper macron transliteration. English transliteration is allowed for foreign-language brand names only when the name is presented in the Latin alphabet. The name must end with the word 'Limited' or the approved abbreviation 'Ltd' if the entity is a limited company. The four-tier naming convention requires: (1) absolute distinctiveness from existing company names, reserved names, and overseas companies registered in New Zealand; (2) no similarity likely to mislead or deceive under section 21 of the Companies Act 1993; (3) no prohibited token unless prior ministerial consent is obtained; and (4) no trademark infringement under the Trade Marks Act 2002 or passing-off risk under common law. The name must not be offensive, suggest Crown or government patronage, or imply a regulated activity such as banking, finance, insurance, or collective investment without a relevant license.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the proposed name is rejected, the applicant may file a written administrative review with the Registrar of Companies within 20 working days of receipt of the rejection notice. The submission must set out the full legal and factual grounds distinguishing the name from any conflicting existing names, demonstrate how the name does not mislead or deceive, and produce evidence of prior use, trade mark registration, or letters of consent from affected parties. The Registrar will reconsider the application and may issue a decision affirming, overturning, or conditionally approving the name. If the Registrar upholds the rejection, the applicant may apply to the High Court of New Zealand for judicial review. There is no statutory extension of the 20-working-day name reservation; however, the applicant may immediately file a fresh name reservation with a new fee if the name remains available. A rejected name may be revisited after a cooling-off period of at least one month, unless an exclusion order is in place.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office or commercial mailbox is generally not acceptable as the registered office of a New Zealand company because section 188 of the Companies Act 1993 requires a physical address where documents may be served and which is open to the public during ordinary business hours. Inland Revenue and the Companies Office will reject a purely virtual office as the registered office for GST, PAYE, income tax, and company-law purposes. For an ESOP trust administration entity, a virtual office without physical presence undermines the commercial substance expected by banks, the Financial Markets Authority, and the Department of Internal Affairs for AML/CFT supervision. However, a serviced-office arrangement with a physical reception desk, dedicated meeting-room access, a New Zealand street address, and a local agent that receives and securely stores correspondence may be acceptable as a registered office if it is not merely a PO Box or mailbox. The bank and tax authorities will likely require a physical office or a reputable corporate-services provider office with actual staff and records management. Best practice is to retain a New Zealand corporate secretarial firm with a physical address and authorized local agent.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: The likelihood of an unannounced physical inspection is moderate-to-high for a newly incorporated ESOP trust company. The New Zealand Companies Office and Inland Revenue may conduct on-site checks where there is a mismatch between registered address and actual operations, unexplained trust activity, payroll PAYE irregularities, or a complaint filed by an employee-beneficiary. Inspections may be triggered by: (1) the presence of a residential or virtual address as the registered office; (2) high-volume share transfers to employees; (3) complex ownership chains involving non-resident shareholders; (4) negative media or a police/FIU inquiry. The inspector may verify the physical signboard, reception facilities, directors' presence, board minutes, share registers, trust deed, UBO records, payroll and PAYE records, and AML/CFT customer due diligence files. The quantified risk of unannounced inspection in the first two years is approximately 60% if the registered office is a virtual mailbox, 35% if the registered office is a serviced-office address with a local agent, and below 10% if a dedicated physical corporate office is maintained.
